answer.rationale: Memory_c6 (multi-year with incumbent, no scope loss) directly applies: finance wants an 18% cut, the primary contract is up, and the line has no buffer so a vendor switch is too risky. I want to verify c6 to confirm the incumbent was actually willing to extend deeper volume pricing without narrowing service scope, since that is the lever that fits the 18% mandate. If the source record confirms the incumbent historically traded term length for price without scope concessions, I'll open a negotiation that asks for both: (1) a longer-term commitment in exchange for an 18% unit-cost reduction, and (2) tighter payment terms, since memory_c4 shows benchmarking drove price AND terms concessions at the last renewal. Memory_c2 is tempting but unsafe here - the line is at 94% with no buffer, so a primary-source migration in 14 days is not credible. Adding a second source (c3) is a structural resilience lever, not a cost lever, and it does not address the 18% mandate on its own. Deferring (c5) does nothing for the spend cut. Renewing incumbent as-is fails the finance mandate outright. One memory verification is sufficient; c6 is the highest-leverage one because it determines whether the cost target is achievable without changing suppliers. Verification budget spent on c6, not c2 or c3, because confirming a vendor switch history would not change the action under current constraints.
